units.title: Loops
units.summary: Iteration in C++: increment and decrement operators, while, do-while and for loops, counters, accumulators, sentinels, nested loops, break and continue, and a light look at file streams.

lessons.title: Increment and decrement operators
lessons.html:
The idea: adding or taking away exactly 1

Programs change a variable by exactly 1 all the time: counting how many numbers were read, moving on to the next item, taking a life away in a game. You can already write that as count = count + 1; or count += 1;. C++ has an even shorter way:

count++;   // add 1 to count
count--;   // subtract 1 from count

++ is the increment operator. To increment means to increase by one. -- is the decrement operator: to decrement means to decrease by one. The variable an operator works on is called its operand. In count++ the operand is count.

If you know Python: Python has no ++ or -- operator, so you write count += 1. In C++ both forms work, and count++ is the one you will see most, especially in loops.

Two ways to write it: prefix and postfix

The operator can go after the variable or before it.

  • Postfix mode: the operator comes after the variable, as in x++ or x--. "Post" means after.
  • Prefix mode: the operator comes before the variable, as in ++x or --x. "Pre" means before.

Written as a statement on its own line, the two modes do exactly the same thing. Both of these lines add 1 to count:

int count = 0;
count++;          // count is 1
++count;          // count is 2

So why have two? Because x++ is also an expression: a piece of code that produces a value, the way x + 1 produces a value. A statement can use that value: store it in another variable, print it, or compare it. That is the only place where prefix and postfix differ.

The value it hands back: old or new

x++ does two jobs at once. It changes x, and it hands back a value for the rest of the statement to use. A change to a variable made while an expression is worked out is called a side effect. Both modes have the same side effect. They differ only in which value they hand back:

WrittenWhat happens to xValue handed back
++xgoes up by 1the new value
x++goes up by 1the old value, what x held before
--xgoes down by 1the new value
x--goes down by 1the old value

A way to remember it: read left to right. In ++x the ++ comes first, so the change comes first and you get the new value. In x++ the variable comes first, so you get x as it is now, and the change follows.

Trace this one line at a time. Each line starts from the values the line before it left.

int x = 5;
int a = x++;   // a gets old x, 5.     then x is 6
int b = ++x;   // x becomes 7 first.   b is 7
int c = x--;   // c gets old x, 7.     then x is 6
int d = --x;   // x becomes 5 first.   d is 5

Notice that x changes on every line, whichever mode is used. The mode only decides what a, b, c and d receive.

The same thing happens when the expression is printed:

int s = 7;
cout << s++ << endl;   // prints 7, then s is 8
cout << s << endl;     // prints 8
int t = 7;
cout << ++t << endl;   // t becomes 8, prints 8

Inside a bigger expression

When x++ sits inside arithmetic, the arithmetic uses the value that x++ hands back. Precedence is the rule for which operator is applied first. ++ and -- have higher precedence than *, /, + and -: they attach to their variable before any arithmetic is done. So p++ * 10 means (p++) * 10.

int p = 3;
int q = p++ * 10;
int r = ++p * 10;
cout << p << " " << q << " " << r;
StatementWhat happenspqr
int p = 3;p starts at 33??
int q = p++ * 10;p++ hands back 3, so q is 3 * 10 = 30. Then p goes up.430?
int r = ++p * 10;p goes up to 5 first, so r is 5 * 10 = 50.53050

The output is 5 30 50. The second line starts from p = 4, not 3, because the first line already changed it.

The decrement works the same way. Write a space between n-- and a minus sign so the two do not run together:

int n = 8;
int m = n-- - 2;          // means (n--) - 2
cout << n << " " << m;   // prints 7 6

n-- hands back the old value 8, so m is 8 - 2 = 6. Then n drops to 7. Getting m = 5 means the 1 was taken away before the subtraction. That is what the prefix form --n - 2 would do.

Inside a loop condition

The next lesson covers the while loop in full. For now you need only this much. while (condition) statement; checks the condition. If it is true, the statement runs once and the condition is checked again. As soon as the condition is false, the loop ends and the program goes on to the next statement.

When the condition contains k++, the comparison uses the old value, and k still goes up by 1 every time the test runs, including the last test, the one that comes out false.

int k = 0;
while (k++ < 2)
    cout << k << " ";
cout << k;
TestCompares old kResultk after the testThen
1st0 < 2true1prints 1
2nd1 < 2true2prints 2
3rd2 < 2false3loop ends

After the loop, cout << k; prints 3, so the output is 1 2 3. Two things catch people. The body prints the new k, one more than the value that was compared. And k ends at 3, not 2, because the false test still added 1.

With prefix, while (++k < 2), k goes up first and the new value is compared: 1 < 2 is true and 1 is printed, then 2 < 2 is false. The output is 1 2.

The operand must be a variable

++ and -- store a new value, so the operand needs a place to store it. C++ calls something that names a storage location you can change an lvalue, because it can appear on the left side of =. An ordinary variable is an lvalue. A number such as 5, or a calculation such as a + b, is only a value. There is nowhere to put the result.

x++;          // fine: x is a variable
5++;          // error: the number 5 cannot change
++(a + b);    // error: a + b is a result, not a variable

g++ reports both errors as lvalue required as increment operand. A named constant such as const int MAX = 10; cannot be incremented either, because const means it may not change. If you want one more than a + b, write a + b + 1.

Do not increment a variable and use it again in the same expression

int r = i++ + ++i;   // do not write this
int w = n * n++;     // or this

You might expect C++ to work from left to right. It does not promise to. C++ does not fix the order in which it works out the two sides of + or *, so nothing says whether the other use of the variable sees the value before or after the change. The result is undefined behavior: the language makes no promise about what happens, and different compilers can give different answers. With -Wall, g++ warns operation on 'i' may be undefined. The code compiles, but the answer cannot be trusted. Put each change in its own statement.

Where you will use them

  • Counting: count++; every time something happens.
  • Loops: the loop lessons in this unit use i++ to move a counter on each time around.
  • For steps other than 1, use combined assignment: x += 2; or x -= 5;.

Mistakes students make

  • Thinking postfix does not change the variable. x++ always adds 1 to x. Postfix only means the expression hands back the old value.
  • Giving the new value to the receiving variable: with x = 5, y = x++; makes y 5, not 6.
  • Starting the next line from the original value instead of the value the previous line left.
  • Reading n-- - 3 as "subtract 1, then subtract 3". The old n is used in the subtraction.
  • Forgetting that the final, false test in while (t++ < 3) still adds 1.
  • Writing 5++ or ++(a + b). The operand must be a variable.
  • Expecting a definite answer from an expression that changes a variable and uses it again, such as i++ + ++i.

What to remember for the test

  • ++ is the increment operator (adds 1). -- is the decrement operator (subtracts 1).
  • Prefix ++x: change first, hand back the new value. Postfix x++: hand back the old value, the variable still changes.
  • As a statement on its own, x++; and ++x; are identical.
  • They bind tighter than arithmetic: a++ * 2 means (a++) * 2.
  • In while (t++ < n) the test compares the old value, and t goes up on every test, the last one included.
  • The operand must be an lvalue (a changeable variable). 5++ and ++(a + b) do not compile.
  • Using ++ or -- on a variable and using that same variable again in the same expression, as in i++ + ++i, is undefined behavior.
  • For a "what does this print" question, keep one column per variable and update it after every statement.

lessons.title: The while loop, input validation and counters
lessons.html:
The idea: do it again while something is true

Suppose a program must print the numbers 1 to 100, or keep asking for an age until the user types a sensible one. Writing the same statement 100 times is not an answer, and you cannot know in advance how many tries the user needs. A loop solves both problems. It is a control structure (a statement, like if, that controls which other statements run and how often) that makes a statement or group of statements run again and again.

The while loop reads almost like English: "while this is true, keep doing this". If you know Python, it is the same idea as Python's while. The differences are spelling: C++ needs parentheses around the condition, and it uses braces { }, not indentation, to mark what is repeated.

The parts of a while loop

while (condition)          // the loop header
{
    statement;             // the body:
    statement;             // what gets repeated
}
  • The loop header is the first line, while (condition). The condition is any true-or-false test, like the ones you wrote for if.
  • The body is the statement, or block of statements in braces, that the loop repeats. It is also called a conditionally executed statement, because it runs only when the condition is true.
  • One pass through the body is one iteration. "How many times does the loop run?" means "how many iterations are there?"

How it runs, step by step

  1. Test the condition.
  2. If it is false, skip the body and carry on with the statement after the loop. The loop is over.
  3. If it is true, run the whole body once, then go back to step 1.
int n = 1;
while (n <= 3)
{
    cout << n << " ";
    n++;
}
cout << "done";
Testnn <= 3?What happens
11trueprints 1, n becomes 2
22trueprints 2, n becomes 3
33trueprints 3, n becomes 4
44falseloop ends

Then done is printed. The output is 1 2 3 done. There were 3 iterations but 4 tests: the last test is the one that comes out false. The condition is checked only at the top. Changing n halfway through the body does not stop the loop on the spot. The rest of the body still runs, and the new value is tested next time round.

Here n is the loop control variable: the variable the condition tests and the body changes, so it decides how many times the loop runs. It needs three things, and a loop goes wrong when one is missing: a starting value before the loop, a test in the header, and a change inside the body that moves it toward making the test false.

A pretest loop can run zero times

The while loop tests before each iteration, so it is called a pretest loop. If the condition is false the very first time, the body never runs at all.

int k = 5, runs = 0;
while (k < 5)       // 5 < 5 is false at once
{
    runs++;
}
cout << runs;       // prints 0

The next lesson covers the do-while loop, which tests after the body and so always runs at least once.

Braces decide what is in the body

Without braces, the body is only the one statement right after the header. Indenting a second line does not put it in the loop. The compiler ignores indentation, unlike Python.

int n = 1;
while (n <= 3)
    cout << n << " ";   // the whole body
    n++;                  // NOT in the loop, despite the indent

The body only prints, n stays 1, and the loop prints 1 1 1 1 without end. The n++ would run once after the loop, but the loop never finishes. Rule: if the body has more than one statement, use braces. Many programmers use them every time.

Infinite loops

An infinite loop is a loop that never stops, because its condition never becomes false. The program seems to freeze, or prints the same thing forever. In a terminal, Ctrl+C stops it. Four causes come up again and again.

1. The control variable never changes. The example above is one: the n++ was outside the loop.

2. A semicolon right after the header.

int i = 0;
while (i < 5);      // this ; is the whole body
{
    cout << i;
    i++;
}

A semicolon on its own is an empty statement: a statement that does nothing. Placed after while (i < 5), it becomes the body. The loop tests 0 < 5, does nothing, tests again, forever. The block in braces is a separate statement that would run after the loop, so it is never reached and nothing is printed.

3. = where == was meant. = stores a value. An assignment is also an expression whose value is the value just stored. In a condition, 0 counts as false and any other number counts as true.

int x = 3;
while (x = 0)       // stores 0 in x. Value 0: false
    cout << "hi";   // never runs
cout << "done";     // prints done

That one skips the body. while (x = 1) does the opposite: it stores 1 every time, 1 counts as true, and the loop never ends. Both compile. g++ with -Wall only warns suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value. To compare, write ==.

4. Testing with != when the steps jump over the target.

int i = 0;
while (i != 10)     // i is 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, ...
    i += 3;         // never exactly 10, so never stops

Write while (i < 10) instead. That stops at 12 after 4 iterations. When the step is bigger than 1, test with <, <=, > or >=, not !=.

Counters

A counter is a variable that counts how many times something happens. It is set to a starting value, usually 0, before the loop, and changed by a fixed amount, usually 1, each time the thing happens. This loop counts how many times 40 can be halved before it reaches 1:

int steps = 0;       // counter starts at 0
int m = 40;
while (m > 1)
{
    m /= 2;          // int division: drops any fraction
    steps++;         // count this halving
}
cout << steps << " " << m;
m at the testm > 1?m after m /= 2steps
40true201
20true102
10true53
5true2 (5 / 2 is 2, not 2.5)4
2true15
1falseloop ends5

The output is 5 1. Dividing two int values throws away the fraction, so a halving loop always reaches 1 and then, if the test allows it, 0. That is how such loops stop.

Always initialize a counter. A local variable that was never given a value holds whatever bits were left in that memory, often called garbage. count++ adds 1 to the garbage, it does not start from 0. Reading a variable that has no value is undefined behavior: the language makes no promise about the result. Write int count = 0;.

Input validation and the priming read

Input validation means checking what the user typed and refusing values that make no sense. A while loop does it well: keep asking while the value is bad.

int age;
cout << "Enter age (0 to 120): ";
cin >> age;                    // the priming read
while (age < 0 || age > 120)   // true while age is BAD
{
    cout << "Invalid. Enter age (0 to 120): ";
    cin >> age;                // read again
}
cout << "Age: " << age;

The read before the loop is the priming read. Like priming a pump, it gets things started: the condition needs a value to test before it can decide whether the loop should run even once. Without it, the first test would look at an age that was never set. The read at the bottom of the body gets each new try, which is tested at the top before the program uses it.

If the user types 150, then -3, then 42: 150 fails the range, so the loop prints the message and reads -3. That fails too, so it prints the message again and reads 42. 42 is in range, the condition is false, the loop ends, and the program prints Age: 42. The condition is written to be true for bad input, using || (or), because the loop should repeat while the value is bad.

Pseudocode and flowcharts

In pseudocode, everything indented under a "While" line is the body. In C++ that means braces around those lines.

Pseudocode              C++
Set n to 5              int n = 5;
While n > 0             while (n > 0)
                        {
    Display n               cout << n << " ";
    Subtract 2 from n       n -= 2;
                        }

This prints 5 3 1: after 1, n becomes -1 and the test fails. "Add k to total" means total += k; and "Add 1 to count" means count++;.

In a flowchart, a rectangle (process box) is an action and a diamond is a yes-or-no decision. A while loop is a diamond with the test, whose Yes arrow runs through the body's boxes and then back up to the diamond. The No arrow leads out of the loop. Because the diamond comes before the body, it is a pretest loop. Example: x starts at 30, the diamond asks "x > 3?", Yes leads to "Display x" and then "Set x to x / 2" (integer division). Displayed: 30, 15, 7. Then x becomes 3, the diamond says No, and 3 is never displayed.

Mistakes students make

  • Assuming the body runs at least once. A while loop whose first test is false runs zero times.
  • Leaving out the braces around a body of two statements, so only the first one repeats.
  • Putting a semicolon right after while (...).
  • Writing = in a condition where == was meant. It compiles.
  • Testing != with a step that can jump over the target.
  • Forgetting to initialize a counter, or forgetting to change the control variable.
  • Leaving out the priming read, or forgetting the second read inside the validation loop, which makes it infinite.
  • Forgetting that int division drops the fraction when tracing a loop such as n /= 2.

What to remember for the test

  • Header, body, iteration: while (cond) is the header, what it repeats is the body, one pass is an iteration.
  • while is a pretest loop: test first, so zero iterations is possible.
  • When a loop ends because its test fails, the number of tests is one more than the number of iterations. The last test is the false one.
  • No braces means only one statement is in the body. Indentation means nothing to the compiler.
  • Infinite loop causes: control variable never changes, ; after the header, = for ==, != with a step that skips the target.
  • Counter: initialize before the loop, change by a fixed step inside it.
  • Validation: priming read before the loop, condition true for bad input, read again inside.
  • To trace any loop, make a table: one row per test, one column per variable.

lessons.title: The do-while loop
lessons.html:
The idea: do it first, then ask

Some jobs must happen once before there is anything to test. A menu has to be shown before the user can choose Quit. "Play again?" can only be asked after one game has been played. A while loop tests first, so it needs a value before the loop starts, which is why the last lesson needed a priming read.

The do-while loop turns the order around: it runs the body first and tests the condition afterwards. Python has no do-while. Python programmers write while True: with a break to get the same effect. C++ has a loop built for it.

The form, and its semicolon

do
{
    statement;
    statement;
} while (condition);   // this semicolon is required

The body sits between do and while. The condition comes last, and the whole thing ends with a semicolon after the closing parenthesis. Leave that semicolon out and the program does not compile. g++ reports something like expected ';' before 'cout'.

This is the exact opposite of the while loop. In a while loop the line while (condition) is the start, and the body still has to follow it. A semicolon there becomes an empty body and causes an infinite loop. In a do-while the line } while (condition); is the end of the statement, so it ends with a semicolon like any other statement.

How it runs

  1. Run the body.
  2. Test the condition.
  3. If it is true, go back to step 1. If it is false, the loop ends.
int n = 1;
do
{
    cout << n << " ";
    n *= 2;
} while (n < 10);
PassBody printsn after the bodyTest n < 10
112true, go again
224true
348true
4816false, loop ends

The output is 1 2 4 8. Each pass ends with exactly one test, so a do-while makes as many tests as it makes iterations.

A posttest loop always runs at least once

Because the test comes after the body, the do-while is a posttest loop. ("Post" means after.) A while loop tests first, so it is a pretest loop. The practical difference shows when the condition is false from the start:

int a = 50;
while (a < 10)           // 50 < 10 is false at once
{
    cout << "W";         // never runs
    a++;
}
int b = 50;
do
{
    cout << "D";         // runs once: prints D
    b++;                 // b is 51
} while (b < 10);        // 51 < 10 is false, loop ends

The while loop prints nothing. The do-while prints D once, because the body ran before anything was tested. The minimum number of iterations of a do-while is therefore 1, and the minimum for a while loop is 0.

whiledo-while
Condition is testedbefore the bodyafter the body
Kind of looppretestposttest
Fewest iterations01
Semicolon after while (...)no (it would empty the body)yes, required
Flowchart diamondat the top, before the bodyat the bottom, after the body

When do the two loops act the same?

If the condition is true at the start, a while loop and a do-while with the same body and condition behave the same. They differ only when the condition is false at the start: the while loop skips the body, the do-while runs it once.

A useful way to see it: a do-while is the body written once on its own, followed by a while loop.

do { BODY } while (COND);

// does exactly the same as

BODY
while (COND) { BODY }

The first copy of the body always runs, then the while loop decides about the rest. This is true for every starting value. Changing the order of the statements inside the body does not give the same loop: k += 2; cout << k; prints the value after the change, so the output shifts.

Where do-while fits: menus and "again?" loops

A user-controlled loop is a loop that keeps going until the user chooses to stop, usually by answering a question. A do-while fits it well, because the answer is read inside the body, before the test needs it.

char again;
do
{
    cout << "Hello!\n";
    cout << "Again? (y/n) ";
    cin >> again;
} while (again == 'y' || again == 'Y');

If the user types y and then n, the body runs twice: once before any test, once more because the first answer was y. The test uses || so that a capital Y also repeats.

Now see what goes wrong with a while loop here:

char again;                            // no value yet
while (again == 'y' || again == 'Y')   // tests garbage
{ ... cin >> again; }

The first test reads again before it has ever been given a value. A local variable with no value holds leftover garbage, so whether the loop runs even once is unpredictable. Reading it is undefined behavior. Two fixes: use a do-while, or give the variable a value before the loop (char again = 'y';, or read it first).

The same shape works for a menu: show the menu, read the choice, act on it, and repeat while the choice is not Quit. It also works for input validation without a priming read:

do
{
    cout << "Enter a positive number: ";
    cin >> num;
} while (num <= 0);    // ask again while the number is bad

Two traps

= instead of ==. In } while (choice = 1); the assignment stores 1 in choice every time, and the value of the assignment is 1. A nonzero value counts as true, so the test is always true. The loop never ends, whatever the user typed, because the typed value is overwritten before it is looked at. It compiles. g++ only warns. Write choice == 1.

A stop value that gets processed. A sentinel is a special input value that means "stop", such as -1. In a do-while the test comes after the body, so the body has already used the sentinel before the loop notices it:

do
{
    cin >> n;
    sum += n;            // the -1 is added too
} while (n != -1);

With input 4 5 -1, sum ends at 4 + 5 + (-1) = 8, not 9. The sentinel lesson later in this unit shows the correct pattern.

Translating "Repeat ... Until"

Pseudocode often writes a posttest loop as Repeat ... Until condition. It runs the body first and stops when the condition becomes true. A C++ do-while keeps going while its condition is true. So the test must be reversed. Opposites: > becomes <=, < becomes >=, == becomes !=. You can also write while (!(condition)).

Set n to 100              int n = 100;
Repeat                    do
                          {
    Display n                 cout << n << " ";
    Set n to n - 30           n -= 30;
Until n < 0               } while (n >= 0);

This prints 100 70 40 10. After 10, n becomes -20, -20 >= 0 is false, and the loop stops. If you copy the Until test unchanged, while (n < 0), the loop stops after printing only 100, because 70 < 0 is false.

Flowchart shape

In a flowchart, a do-while has the process boxes (rectangles) first and the decision diamond at the bottom. The diamond's Yes arrow goes back up to the first box of the body, and No leads on. A while loop has its diamond at the top, before the body. Look for where the diamond is, and you know which loop it is.

A preview: the for loop is also a pretest loop

The next lesson covers the for loop. You may meet one before then, so here is enough to read it. for (int n = 1; n > 50; n *= 3) sets n to 1 once, then tests n > 50 before every pass, like a while loop, and does n *= 3 after each pass. Here 1 > 50 is false at the first test, so its body never runs.

Mistakes students make

  • Leaving off the semicolon after } while (condition). It is a compile error.
  • Thinking the condition is checked before the first pass. It is not, so the body runs at least once even when the condition starts out false.
  • Copying a "Repeat ... Until" test straight into while (...) instead of reversing it.
  • Testing a variable in a while loop before it has a value, when a do-while would read it first.
  • Writing while (choice = 1); instead of ==, which never ends.
  • Assuming that a while loop and a do-while always act the same. They differ when the condition starts out false.

What to remember for the test

  • do-while: body first, then test. It is a posttest loop and runs at least once.
  • Form: do { ... } while (condition); with a required semicolon at the end.
  • A do-while equals one copy of the body followed by a while loop with the same body and condition.
  • Best fit: menus, "run again?" questions and other user-controlled loops, where the body must run before the test makes sense.
  • "Repeat ... Until X" becomes do { ... } while (!(X));, so reverse the test.
  • Flowchart: diamond at the bottom means do-while, diamond at the top means while.
  • To trace it, run the body first, then write the variables and the test result after each pass.

lessons.title: The for loop
lessons.html:
The idea: a loop that counts

Loops come in two kinds, depending on whether you know in advance how many times they will run.

  • A conditional loop repeats while some condition holds, and nobody knows beforehand how many passes that will take. "Keep asking until the password is right" is one. The while and do-while loops in the last two lessons were mostly of this kind.
  • A count-controlled loop repeats a specific number of times that is known before the loop starts: print 10 lines, read 5 scores, count down from 3.

A count-controlled loop always needs the same three things: initialize a counter, test the counter against a limit, and update the counter on every pass. With a while loop those three are spread out: one before the loop, one in the header, one at the bottom of the body. The for loop puts all three in one header line, where you can see them at once.

If you know Python: for i in range(4): becomes for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) in C++. range(a, b, s) with a positive step s becomes for (int i = a; i < b; i += s). The C++ form is more general, because the test and the update can be anything.

The header

for (initialization; test; update)
    statement;
  • The initialization expression sets the counter's starting value, as in int i = 0.
  • The test expression is the condition that decides whether the body runs (again), as in i < 4.
  • The update expression changes the counter after each pass, as in i++.

Two semicolons separate the three parts. There is no semicolon after the update, and none after the closing parenthesis. As with while, a body of more than one statement needs braces.

The order things happen

  1. The initialization runs, once.
  2. The test is checked. If it is false, the loop ends.
  3. The body runs.
  4. The update runs.
  5. Back to step 2.
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)
    cout << i << " ";
StepiWhat happens
initialization0i is created and set to 0
test 0 < 40true: body prints 0, then update makes i 1
test 1 < 41true: prints 1, i becomes 2
test 2 < 42true: prints 2, i becomes 3
test 3 < 43true: prints 3, i becomes 4
test 4 < 44false: loop ends

The output is 0 1 2 3. Count the parts: the initialization ran 1 time, the test 5 times, the body 4 times and the update 4 times. The test always runs one more time than the body, because the last test is the one that fails.

The test comes before the body, so the for loop is a pretest loop, like while. for (int i = 5; i < 3; i++) never runs its body, because 5 < 3 is false at the first test.

The same loop written with while

int i = 0;                // initialization: before the loop
while (i < 4)             // test
{
    cout << i << " ";     // body
    i++;                  // update: at the END of the body
}

This prints 0 1 2 3 too. The update must go last in the body. Put i++ before the cout and the loop prints 1 2 3 4, because each value is printed after it has changed.

How many times does it run?

  • for (i = a; i < b; i++) runs b - a times. From 0 to below 10 is 10 times.
  • for (i = a; i <= b; i++) runs b - a + 1 times. From 1 to 10 inclusive is 10 times.
  • With a step other than 1, list the values. for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i += 5) visits 1, 6, 11, 16. The next value, 21, fails the test. So it runs 4 times and prints 1 6 11 16.

Notice in the last example that the last value printed is 16, but the value of i when the loop ends is 21: the first value that failed.

Counting down, and other steps

for (int i = 5; i >= 1; i--)      // prints 5 4 3 2 1
    cout << i << " ";
for (int p = 1; p < 100; p *= 2)  // prints 1 2 4 8 16 32 64
    cout << p << " ";

When counting down, pick the test with care. i >= 1 is still true at 1, so 1 is printed. i > 1 stops before 1 and prints 5 4 3 2. i <= 1 is false at the start (5 is not at most 1), so nothing prints. A step that moves away from the limit, such as starting at 1 with i-- and testing i <= 10, never makes the test false.

Scope: where the counter exists

A variable's scope is the stretch of code in which its name can be used. A variable declared in the initialization part, such as int i = 0, exists only inside the loop: in the header and the body. After the loop the name is gone.

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }
cout << i;     // error: 'i' was not declared in this scope

If you need the counter after the loop, declare it before the loop and only give it a value in the initialization part:

int x;
for (x = 1; x < 10; x += 4) { }   // empty body: the loop only moves x
cout << x;                        // prints 13

x takes 1, 5, 9, then 13 fails the test. The loop stops with x at 13, and x still exists, so 13 is printed.

The same rule covers any variable declared inside the braces of a loop body, in a for, while or do-while loop. You may declare variables there, but they exist only inside that block. Using the name after the closing brace is a compile error.

Several variables, and empty parts

The initialization and update parts may each hold several expressions separated by commas. The test is still a single condition.

for (int a = 1, b = 10; a < b; a += 2, b -= 2)
    cout << a << "-" << b << " ";

The pairs are (1, 10), (3, 8), (5, 6). Next comes (7, 4), and 7 < 4 is false. Output: 1-10 3-8 5-6.

Any of the three parts may be left out, but both semicolons must stay.

int j = 2;
for ( ; j < 30; )     // no initialization, no update
    j *= 2;           // so the body must change j
cout << j;            // j went 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Prints 32

A missing test counts as true, so for (;;) runs forever unless something inside the body stops it, such as a break statement (covered later in this unit) or a return.

Traps

A semicolon after the header. It becomes an empty body, as with while.

int hits = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++);   // body is the lone ;
    hits++;                     // runs once, after the loop
cout << hits;                   // prints 1

The loop does nothing 5 times and ends. The indented line is not in the loop, it runs once afterwards. The loop is not infinite, because the update still runs.

Changing the counter in the body as well as in the update.

for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++)
{
    cout << i << " ";
    i++;               // extra change
}                      // prints 0 2 4 6

Each pass adds 1 in the body and 1 more in the update, so i goes 0, 2, 4, 6, then 8 fails. Half the values are skipped. In a loop meant to read 8 numbers, only 4 would be read. Change a for loop's counter only in the update part.

Flowchart of a for loop

A for loop is drawn like a while loop: a process box sets the counter, then a diamond holds the test. The Yes arrow runs through the body's boxes, then through a box for the update, and back up to the diamond. The No arrow leaves the loop. The order of the boxes matters: body first, update second.

Mistakes students make

  • Thinking the update runs before the body on the first pass. The first pass uses the starting value.
  • Using the counter after the loop when it was declared in the header.
  • Off-by-one tests: < where <= was needed, or the other way round.
  • Counting down with the wrong test, such as i <= 1 when starting at 10.
  • Putting a semicolon after for (...).
  • Changing the counter inside the body as well as in the update.
  • Writing n + 5 as the update. That works out a value but stores nothing, so n never changes. Write n += 5.

What to remember for the test

  • for (initialization; test; update). Initialization runs once. Then test, body, update, test, body, update, and so on.
  • The for loop is a pretest loop. The test runs once more than the body.
  • i = a; i < b runs b - a times. With <=, b - a + 1 times. With another step, list the values.
  • A counter declared in the header, or any variable declared inside a loop body, does not exist after the loop.
  • Commas allow several initializations and updates. Any part can be empty. for (;;) is infinite.
  • Count-controlled loop: known number of passes, usually a for. Conditional loop: unknown number of passes, usually a while or do-while.

lessons.title: Accumulators, sentinels and choosing a loop
lessons.html:
The idea: loops that add things up

Most useful loops do something with each value they see: add it to a total, count it, work out an average at the end. This lesson covers three ideas that go with that: keeping a running total, stopping a list of unknown length with a sentinel, and choosing which of the three loops to use.

Running totals and accumulators

A running total is a sum that grows each time the loop body runs. The variable that holds it is called an accumulator, because it accumulates (collects) the values. The pattern always has three steps:

  1. Before the loop, set the accumulator to a starting value. For a sum that is 0.
  2. Inside the loop, add each new value: total += value;
  3. After the loop, use the result.
int sum = 0;                        // step 1
for (int i = 2; i <= 8; i += 2)
    sum += i;                       // step 2
cout << sum;                        // step 3: prints 20
isum beforesum += isum after
200 + 22
422 + 46
666 + 612
81212 + 820

An accumulator is not the same as a counter. A counter goes up by a fixed amount, usually 1 (count++), to record how many times something happened. An accumulator goes up by whatever the current value is (sum += i). Many loops keep both.

Why the starting value matters. The first pass combines the starting value with the first real value, so the start must be a value that changes nothing. Adding 0 changes nothing, so a sum starts at 0. Multiplying by 1 changes nothing, so a product starts at 1.

int prod = 1;
for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++)
    prod *= i;          // 1*1=1, 1*2=2, 2*3=6, 6*4=24
cout << prod;           // prints 24

Start prod at 0 and every multiplication gives 0, so it prints 0. Start it at 5 and the answer is 5 times too big, 120. Leave it with no value and it starts from garbage: whatever bits were left in that memory. *= and += always use the old value, so a bad start is never overwritten.

Declare the accumulator before the loop. Declared inside the body, it would be set back to 0 on every pass, and it would not exist after the loop.

Averages and integer division

An average is the sum divided by the count. If both are int, C++ does integer division and drops the fraction: 17 / 4 is 4, not 4.25. Convert one of them to double first: static_cast<double>(17) / 4 is 4.25. Also make sure the count is not 0 before dividing.

Sentinels: lists of unknown length

Suppose the user types in test scores, and the program does not know how many there will be. One way to mark the end is a sentinel: a special value that means "the list is over". It is not real data, so it must be a value that real data can never take. Scores are never negative, so -1 works for scores.

The safe pattern is the priming read from the while loop lesson:

int n, sum = 0;
cin >> n;              // priming read
while (n != -1)        // stop at the sentinel
{
    sum += n;          // process the value
    cin >> n;          // read the next value LAST
}
cout << sum;

Trace it with the input 5 8 3 -1:

n just readn != -1?sum after the body
5 (priming read)true5
8true13
3true16
-1falseloop ends, sum stays 16

It prints 16. The key is the order inside the body: the read is the last statement, so every new value goes straight to the test before anything is done with it. When the sentinel arrives, the test stops the loop before the sentinel can be added.

Two more things to notice. If the very first value is the sentinel, the loop runs zero times and the sum is 0, which is correct, because the while loop tests first. And anything typed after the sentinel is never read at all.

The wrong way: a do-while.

do
{
    cin >> n;
    sum += n;          // adds before the test looks at n
} while (n != -1);

With the same input 5 8 3 -1, this reads -1, adds it, and only then tests. The sum is 5 + 8 + 3 + (-1) = 15, one too small. The sentinel was processed as data, which is exactly what a sentinel must not be.

A full example with a counter, an accumulator and an average:

int score, total = 0, count = 0;
cin >> score;
while (score != -1)
{
    total += score;    // accumulator
    count++;           // counter
    cin >> score;
}
if (count > 0)
    cout << fixed << setprecision(2)
         << static_cast<double>(total) / count;

With input 90 85 72 -1: total is 247, count is 3, and it prints 82.33. Without the cast, 247 / 3 would give 82.

Pseudocode often describes the same pattern: "Input value. While value is not 0: add value to sum, input value." The first "Input value" is the priming read, and 0 is the sentinel.

Another way: ask how many first

The program can also ask the user how many values there are, and use that number as the limit of a for loop:

int count, value, total = 0;
cin >> count;                    // how many values?
for (int i = 1; i <= count; i++)
{
    cin >> value;
    total += value;
}
cout << total;

With input 3 and then 7 -2 5, the loop runs 3 times and prints 7 + (-2) + 5 = 10. The user decides the count, but the loop itself is count-controlled: the count is known before the loop starts. Here there is no sentinel, so every value is data, negative ones included. With a sentinel, -1 means stop. With a counted loop, -1 is just another number to add.

Choosing a loop

Any of the three loops can be made to do any job. The choice is about which one says what you mean most clearly.

LoopTestsFewest passesBest when
forbefore the body0The number of passes is known before the loop starts: exactly 30 scores, the numbers 1 to 100, a count the user typed in.
whilebefore the body0The loop may need to run zero times and the number of passes is unknown: input validation, reading until a sentinel.
do-whileafter the body1The body must run at least once: menus, "again?" questions.

Both for and while are pretest loops, so either one runs zero times when its test is false at the start. for (int i = 10; i < 5; i++) never runs its body. The while and do-while loops are the conditional loops. The for loop is the natural count-controlled loop, because its header keeps the initialization, test and update in one place.

You will also meet nested loops, a loop inside another loop, in the next lesson. They are for jobs where each pass contains a repeated job of its own, such as rows and columns. A single list of values needs only one loop.

Mistakes students make

  • Forgetting to set the accumulator to 0 (or 1 for a product) before the loop.
  • Starting a product at 0, which makes the answer 0.
  • Declaring the accumulator inside the loop body, so it resets every pass.
  • Adding the sentinel to the total, which is what a do-while sentinel loop does.
  • Putting the second read at the top of the while body instead of the bottom, which skips the first value and processes the sentinel.
  • Choosing a sentinel that could be real data, such as 0 in a list where 0 is a valid value.
  • Dividing two ints for an average and losing the fraction.

What to remember for the test

  • Running total: the sum. Accumulator: the variable that holds it. Set it before the loop: 0 for sums, 1 for products.
  • Sentinel: a special end-of-list value that is never real data.
  • Sentinel pattern: priming read, while (value != sentinel), process, read again as the last statement.
  • A do-while sentinel loop processes the sentinel. A while loop with a priming read does not.
  • A counted loop (read the count, then a for loop) treats every value as data.
  • for: known count. while: may run zero times, unknown count. do-while: at least once.
  • To trace an accumulator, write one row per pass: the value, the total before, the total after.

lessons.title: Nested loops, break and continue
lessons.book: Sections 5.10 and 5.12, pages 272 to 275 and 294 to 296
lessons.html:
The idea: repetition inside repetition

Some jobs repeat a job that itself repeats. A clock: for each hour, the minutes go round from 0 to 59. A table: for each row, print every column. A nested loop is a loop placed inside the body of another loop. The one on the outside is the outer loop, the one inside is the inner loop.

This lesson also covers two statements that change the normal flow of any loop: break, which leaves a loop early, and continue, which skips to the next pass.

How a nested loop runs

One rule explains everything: each time the outer loop makes one pass, the inner loop starts again from its beginning and runs all of its passes. Only when the inner loop has finished does the outer loop move on to its next pass.

for (int i = 1; i <= 2; i++)
{
    for (int j = 1; j <= 3; j++)
        cout << i << j << " ";
    cout << endl;            // after the inner loop: ends the row
}
Outer passInner loop doesThen
i = 1j = 1, 2, 3: prints 11 12 13. j = 4 fails.new line
i = 2j starts again at 1: prints 21 22 23. j = 4 fails.new line
i = 33 <= 2 is false: the outer loop ends.nothing
11 12 13
21 22 23

Look at how the two counters move. j runs through all its values while i stays the same. i changes only once per full run of the inner loop. The inner counter changes fastest, like the second hand of a clock, which goes all the way round for each single step of the minute hand.

Give each loop its own counter name, such as i and j. If the inner loop changed the outer loop's counter, both loops would go wrong.

Where the newline goes

In the example, cout << endl; sits inside the outer loop's braces but after the inner loop. So it runs once per outer pass, and each row ends up on its own line. Move it inside the inner loop's body and every single value goes on its own line. Move it after both loops and everything prints on one line. When reading nested code, check which braces each statement is inside.

Counting the passes

When the inner loop always runs the same number of times, multiply. An outer loop of 2 passes with an inner loop of 5 passes runs the inner body 2 x 5 = 10 times, not 2 + 5 = 7. The inner loop does its 5 passes once for every outer pass.

int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < 5; j++)
        count++;
cout << count;        // prints 10

When the inner limit depends on the outer counter, add the rows. Here the inner loop runs r times, and r changes:

for (int r = 3; r >= 1; r--)
{
    for (int c = 1; c <= r; c++)
        cout << '#';
    cout << '\n';
}

Row 1 has r = 3, so 3 marks. Then 2, then 1. Output:

###
##
#

The inner body ran 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 times. You cannot multiply here, because each row has a different length.

Pseudocode for nested loops reads the same way. "For row from 1 to 3" becomes for (int row = 1; row <= 3; row++). "From 1 to row" includes row, so its test is <= row. Each "End For" closes the body of its own loop, so a line between the inner "End For" and the outer "End For" runs once per outer pass.

break: leave the loop now

You met break in the switch statement. Inside a loop, break; ends the loop at once. The rest of the body is skipped, the update does not run, the test is not checked again, and the program carries on with the first statement after the loop. It is almost always inside an if.

int i;
for (i = 1; i <= 10; i++)
{
    if (i * i > 50)
        break;
    cout << i << " ";
}
cout << "| i = " << i;

For i = 1 to 7, the square is at most 49, so each value is printed. At i = 8, 64 > 50, so break runs. The cout below it is skipped, and so is i++. The program prints 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 | i = 8. Compare: if the loop had ended normally, i would hold 11, the first value that failed i <= 10. After a break, the counter keeps the value it had when the break ran.

In nested loops, break leaves only the innermost loop that contains it. The outer loop carries on with its next pass, and the inner loop starts fresh on that pass.

for (int a = 1; a <= 2; a++)
{
    for (int b = 1; b <= 5; b++)
    {
        if (b == 3)
            break;             // leaves the b loop only
        cout << a << b << " ";
    }
    cout << "/ ";              // still runs, every outer pass
}

Output: 11 12 / 21 22 / . Each inner run prints b = 1 and 2, then stops at 3. The outer loop still makes both of its passes. To leave both loops at once, a program usually sets a flag (a bool variable) before the break and has the outer loop test it.

continue: skip to the next pass

continue; skips the rest of the current pass only. The loop does not end. Where it jumps depends on the loop:

  • In a for loop, it jumps to the update expression, then the test. The update still happens.
  • In a while or do-while loop, it jumps straight to the test. There is no separate update part, so anything in the body after the continue is skipped, including an update written there.
for (int q = 1; q <= 7; q++)
{
    if (q % 3 == 0)
        continue;          // skip multiples of 3
    cout << q << " ";
}                          // prints 1 2 4 5 7

When q is 3 or 6, the cout is skipped, but q++ still runs, so the loop moves on normally.

The while loop trap.

int k = 0;
while (k < 4)
{
    if (k == 1)
        continue;   // jumps to the test: k++ below is skipped
    cout << k;
    k++;
}

When k reaches 1, continue jumps back to the test. k++ never runs, so k stays 1, the test is true again, and the same thing happens forever: an infinite loop. The fix is to change k before the continue can skip the update: write if (k == 1) { k++; continue; }. Now the pass for 1 moves k on without printing, and the loop prints 023. Another way is to update inside the condition, as in while (k++ < 4), so the update runs at every test. That also changes which values the body sees, so trace it again.

breakcontinue
Ends the loop?Yes, at onceNo, only the current pass
Goes next tothe first statement after the loopfor: the update, then the test. while and do-while: the test
In nested loopsleaves the innermost loop onlyaffects the innermost loop only

Both make a loop harder to follow, because the body no longer always runs from top to bottom. Use them sparingly.

Mistakes students make

  • Adding the two loop counts (4 + 3) instead of multiplying them (4 x 3).
  • Multiplying when the inner limit depends on the outer counter. Add the rows instead.
  • Thinking the inner loop carries on from where it stopped. It starts again from its initialization on every outer pass.
  • Thinking the outer counter changes faster. The inner counter changes fastest.
  • Thinking break leaves every loop. It leaves only the innermost one.
  • Mixing up break (end the loop) and continue (skip to the next pass).
  • Thinking continue skips the update of a for loop. It does not. It does skip an update written in a while loop's body.
  • Forgetting that after a break the counter is not updated again.

What to remember for the test

  • Nested loop: for each outer pass, the inner loop runs completely, starting from scratch.
  • Total inner passes: multiply when the inner count is fixed, add row by row when it depends on the outer counter.
  • The inner counter changes fastest.
  • break: leave the innermost loop now. The rest of the body and the update are skipped.
  • continue: skip the rest of this pass. A for loop then runs its update and test. A while or do-while goes straight to the test.
  • A continue that skips a while loop's update makes an infinite loop.
  • To trace nested loops, write one line per inner pass with both counters, and mark where each inner loop ends.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files (not on syllabus)
lessons.html:
The idea: data that outlives the program

This section is outside the course syllabus, so you need the vocabulary and the basic pattern, not every detail. A few questions do test it.

Everything a program keeps in variables disappears when it ends. To keep data for next time, or to read a long list of numbers without typing them, a program uses a file on the disk. C++ handles files with the same tools you already use for the keyboard and the screen.

A stream is a flow of characters going into or out of a program. cin is a stream that flows in from the keyboard. cout is a stream that flows out to the screen. A file stream is a stream connected to a file instead. Once it is connected, you use >> and << on it exactly as you do on cin and cout.

The two file stream types

Both come from the header <fstream> (file stream), so a program that uses files starts with #include <fstream> as well as #include <iostream>.

TypeStands forJobWorks like
ofstreamoutput file streamwrites data into a filecout, with <<
ifstreaminput file streamreads data from a filecin, with >>

Read the first letter: o for output, i for input. "Output" is from the program's point of view: data goes out of the program into the file.

Do not confuse them with istream, the general input stream type that cin belongs to, or with iostream, the header you include to get cin and cout. Neither of those opens a file.

Three steps: open, use, close

1. Open. Declare a stream variable and connect it to a file with the open member function. (A member function is a function that belongs to an object and is called with a dot, like cin.ignore().) You can also give the file name when you declare the stream.

ofstream outFile;
outFile.open("scores.txt");     // two steps
ifstream inFile("scores.txt");  // or one step

2. Use. Write with << or read with >>.

3. Close. Call close() when you are done: outFile.close();. Output is held in memory (a buffer) and written to the disk in chunks. Closing makes sure everything still waiting in the buffer is actually written, and it releases the file so other code can use it. Always close a file when you have finished with it.

What open does to the file

  • An ofstream opening a file that does not exist creates it, empty.
  • An ofstream opening a file that already exists erases its old contents and starts it empty. That is the default. (Adding to the end of a file instead needs a different open mode, which this course does not require.) Python's open(name, "w") behaves the same way.
  • An ifstream opening a file that does not exist fails: there is nothing to read. Python would stop with an error here. C++ does not stop. The stream just goes into a fail state, so the program must check.
ifstream inFile("scores.txt");
if (!inFile)                    // true if the open failed
{
    cout << "Could not open scores.txt\n";
    return 1;
}

inFile.fail() asks the same question in words: it is true when the open failed.

The read position

An input file stream keeps a read position: the next byte (character) it will read. When the file is opened, the read position is at the first byte of the file. Each read moves it forward past what was read, so the next read picks up where the last one stopped. This is the same idea as the keyboard input buffer, where each cin >> starts where the previous one stopped.

Reading until the end of the file

A program usually does not know how many values a file holds. The standard loop is:

int value, total = 0, count = 0;
while (inFile >> value)     // read, then test whether it worked
{
    total += value;
    count++;
}
inFile.close();

Why this works: the expression inFile >> value does two things. It tries to read a value, and then it counts as true if the read worked and false if it failed. At the end of the file there is nothing left to read, so the read fails and the loop ends. The read is in the condition, so every value is tested before the body uses it. It plays the part of both the priming read and the read at the bottom of the body.

A complete example

#include <iostream>
#include <fstream>
using namespace std;

int main()
{
    ofstream outFile("scores.txt");   // create the file
    outFile << 90 << endl;
    outFile << 75 << endl;
    outFile << 82 << endl;
    outFile.close();                  // make sure it is written

    ifstream inFile("scores.txt");    // read it back
    if (!inFile)
    {
        cout << "Could not open the file\n";
        return 1;
    }
    int value, total = 0, count = 0;
    while (inFile >> value)
    {
        total += value;
        count++;
    }
    inFile.close();
    cout << count << " values, total " << total << endl;
    return 0;
}

This prints 3 values, total 247. The summing loop is the same accumulator loop as before. Only the source of the data changed, from cin to inFile.

Mistakes students make

  • Mixing up the types: ifstream is for reading, ofstream is for writing.
  • Forgetting #include <fstream>.
  • Using << on an ifstream, or >> on an ofstream. Neither compiles. You read with >> and write with <<, just as with cin and cout.
  • Expecting an ofstream to keep a file's old contents. By default it erases them.
  • Reading from a file without checking that it opened.
  • Forgetting to close() the file.

What to remember for the test

  • Header <fstream>. ofstream writes (output), ifstream reads (input).
  • Open, use with << or >>, then close(). Closing writes out anything still buffered.
  • ofstream: creates a missing file, erases an existing one. ifstream: fails on a missing file, so check with if (!inFile).
  • The read position starts at the first byte and moves forward with each read.
  • while (inFile >> value) reads every value until the end of the file.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain:
Postfix `x++` hands back the old value of x, and then x goes up by 1.
```
int x = 5      x is 5
int y = x++    y gets the old value, 5. Then x becomes 6
```
The output prints x first, then y, so it is `6 5`. If you answered `6 6`, you gave y the new value, which is what `y = ++x;` would do. If you answered `5 5`, remember that `x++` always changes x. Postfix only decides that y receives the value from before the change.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain:
Keep a running value for a and update it after every statement.
```
int a = 4          a is 4
int b = a++ * 2    a++ hands back 4, so b = 4 * 2 = 8. a is now 5
int c = ++a * 2    ++a makes a 6 first, so c = 6 * 2 = 12
```
The output lists a, b and c: `6 8 12`. The usual slip is forgetting that the first line already changed a to 5, so `++a` starts from 5, not 4. Another is printing a as 4 or 5: both lines add 1 to a, so it ends at 6.

questions.prompt: After this code runs, what are the values of n and m?
choices: n is 9 and m is 7
n is 10 and m is 7
n is 9 and m is 6
n is 10 and m is 6
questions.explain:
`n-- - 3` is read as `(n--) - 3`: a postfix decrement, then an ordinary subtraction.
```
n-- hands back the old value   10
m = 10 - 3                     m is 7
n has 1 taken away             n is 9
```
So n is 9 and m is 7. "m is 6" comes from taking the 1 away before the subtraction, which is what the prefix form `--n - 3` would do. "n is 10" forgets that postfix still decreases n. Postfix only decides that the subtraction gets the old value.

questions.prompt: As complete statements by themselves, `count++;` and `++count;` have exactly the same effect on count.
questions.explain: True. As a statement by itself, `count++;` and `++count;` both add 1 to count, and nothing else happens. The two modes differ only in the value the expression hands back: postfix gives the old value, prefix gives the new one. On a line by itself nothing uses that value, so the two are identical. The difference shows only when the value is used, as in `y = count++;` or `cout << ++count;`.

questions.prompt: The `--` operator is called the ____ operator.
questions.explain: `--` is the decrement operator. To decrement means to decrease by one, so `lives--;` does the same as `lives = lives - 1;`. Its partner `++` is the increment operator, which adds 1. Both come in a prefix form (`--lives`) and a postfix form (`lives--`).

questions.prompt: Why is the statement `int r = i++ + ++i;` a bad idea?
choices: Postfix and prefix operators cannot appear in the same statement by rule of syntax
It modifies i twice in one expression with no defined order, so the result is not reliable
It always evaluates to 0
It is fine; C++ evaluates strictly left to right so the result is well-defined
questions.explain:
In `i++ + ++i`, i is changed twice inside one expression. C++ does not fix the order in which it works out the two sides of `+`, so nothing says which value of i each side sees. That is undefined behavior: there is no reliable result, and different compilers can give different numbers. g++ with -Wall warns "operation on 'i' may be undefined".

The other choices are wrong. The statement does compile, since no rule forbids prefix and postfix in one statement. It does not always give 0, or any fixed number. And C++ does not promise strict left-to-right order here, which is exactly why the result cannot be trusted. Fix it by putting each change in its own statement.

questions.prompt: The statement `5++;` is legal because 5 is a value that can be increased.
questions.explain: False. `++` has to store the new value somewhere, so its operand must be a variable: a storage location that can be changed, which C++ calls an lvalue. 5 is a literal, a fixed number with nowhere to keep a 6, so `5++;` does not compile. g++ says "lvalue required as increment operand". To get 6, write `5 + 1`, or put 5 in a variable and increment that: `int n = 5; n++;`.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain:
Track n at each test. The body prints `n * n`, the square of n, then adds 1 to n.
```
n = 1   1 <= 4 true    prints 1
n = 2   2 <= 4 true    prints 4
n = 3   3 <= 4 true    prints 9
n = 4   4 <= 4 true    prints 16
n = 5   5 <= 4 false   loop ends
```
After the loop, `end` is printed. Output: `1 4 9 16 end`. Two slips to avoid: printing n instead of its square, and printing 25. When n is 5 the test fails before the body can run.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body of this loop run?
choices: It is an infinite loop
questions.explain:
Zero. A while loop tests its condition before the body. The first test is `10 > 10`, and 10 is not greater than itself, so the test is false at once. The body is skipped completely and `runs` stays 0.

"1" assumes the body always runs at least once, which is true of a do-while loop, not a while loop. "10" assumes the loop counts k down from 10. "It is an infinite loop" is wrong too: a loop whose first test is false ends immediately.

questions.prompt: A while loop is a pretest loop: its condition is evaluated before each execution of the body, so the body might never execute.
questions.explain: True. A while loop checks its condition first, before every iteration. If the condition is false the very first time, the body is skipped and runs zero times. For example, `int n = 5; while (n < 3) cout << n;` prints nothing. That is what "pretest" means. The do-while loop is the posttest version: it runs the body first and tests afterwards, so its body always runs at least once.

questions.prompt: Why does this program never finish?
choices: i is declared as int instead of unsigned
The braces must come before the condition
cout cannot be used inside a while loop
The semicolon after the condition makes the loop body empty, so i never changes
questions.explain:
Look at the end of the header: `while (i < 5);`. A semicolon on its own is an empty statement, a statement that does nothing, and it becomes the entire body. The loop tests `0 < 5`, does nothing, tests again, forever. i never changes because `i++` is not in the loop. The block in braces is a separate statement after the loop, so it is never reached and nothing is printed.

The other explanations are wrong: int works fine for a counter, the braces correctly come after the header, and cout can be used inside any loop. The fix is to delete that semicolon.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
choices: done
hihihi... forever
hidone
The code does not compile
questions.explain:
`x = 0` uses one equals sign, so it is an assignment, not a comparison. It stores 0 in x, and the value of the whole assignment is 0. In a condition, 0 counts as false. So the very first test is false, the body is skipped, and the program goes on to print `done`.

"hi forever" would happen with a nonzero value such as `while (x = 1)`, because any nonzero value counts as true. "hidone" assumes the body runs once, but it never runs. The code does compile: g++ only warns "suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value". To compare, write `x == 0`.

questions.prompt: The user types 120, then -5, then 88. What does this program print?
questions.explain:
The condition is true while the score is BAD (below 0 or above 100), so each bad value prints `bad` and reads again.
```
cin >> score     score = 120   (the priming read)
test 120         120 > 100, bad   prints bad, reads -5
test -5          -5 < 0, bad      prints bad, reads 88
test 88          in range         condition false, loop ends
cout << score    prints 88
```
Each `bad` is followed by `\n`, so the output is three lines: `bad`, `bad`, `88`.

questions.prompt: In an input validation loop, why is the first value read BEFORE the while statement?
choices: while loops cannot contain cin
The condition needs a value to test before the loop can decide whether to run
It makes the loop run faster
The value must be read twice to be stored
questions.explain:
The while loop tests its condition before it runs the body even once. To test whether the value is valid, there must already be a value. The priming read before the loop supplies it, and the read inside the loop supplies each later try. Without the priming read, the first test would look at a variable that was never given a value.

The other reasons are false. cin works inside a while loop, and the second read sits inside the body. Reading first has nothing to do with speed. And the value is not read twice to store it once: each read stores a new value typed by the user.

questions.prompt: The only statement in a loop body that touches `passes` is `passes++;`, and `passes` starts at 0. After the loop, it tells how many times the body ran. What is this kind of variable called?
questions.explain: It is a counter: a variable that counts how many times something happens. It starts at a known value before the loop, here 0, and changes by a fixed amount each time, here `passes++` adds 1 per iteration. So after the loop, `passes` holds the number of times the body ran. For example, if the body ran 4 times, passes is 4. A counter must be initialized, or `++` adds 1 to garbage.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain:
Make a table. Remember that `n /= 2` is integer division, so any fraction is dropped.
```
n at test   n > 1?   n after /= 2   c
100         true     50             1
50          true     25             2
25          true     12             3   (not 12.5)
12          true     6              4
6           true     3              5
3           true     1              6   (not 1.5)
1           false    loop ends
```
Output: `6 1`. If you got `7 0`, you let the loop run once more. That would happen with `n > 0`, but `1 > 1` is false, so the loop stops with n at 1.

questions.prompt: What happens when this loop runs?
choices: It stops when i equals 10
It stops after 4 iterations
It never stops, because i jumps from 9 to 12 and never equals 10
It does not compile because != is invalid in a while
questions.explain:
It never stops. i goes 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and so on. It jumps from 9 straight to 12, so it is never exactly 10, and `i != 10` is true forever.

"It stops when i equals 10" assumes i lands on 10, which it never does. "It stops after 4 iterations" is wrong too: after 4 iterations i is 12, and 12 is not 10, so the loop keeps going. And `!=` is perfectly valid in a while condition. The fix is to test `i < 10`, which does stop at 12 after 4 iterations.

questions.prompt: If a while loop's body has two statements and the braces are left off, both statements are still part of the loop.
questions.explain:
False. Without braces, the body of a while loop is only the one statement right after the header. The second statement is outside the loop, even if it is indented to look like part of it. The C++ compiler ignores indentation, unlike Python.
```
while (n <= 3)
    cout << n;    // the whole body
    n++;          // after the loop, not in it
```
Here n never changes inside the loop, so it runs forever. Braces around both statements fix it.

questions.prompt:
Pseudocode:
Set count to 0
While count < 3
  Display count * 2
  Add 1 to count
Which C++ matches it?
questions.explain:
The pseudocode starts count at 0, tests `count < 3`, and repeats two indented lines. In C++ both lines must sit inside braces. The matching code is `int count = 0;` then `while (count < 3)` with a braced body holding the `cout` and `count++`. It prints `0 2 4`.

The version without braces repeats only the `cout`. count never changes, so it prints 0 forever. The `count <= 3` version runs one extra time and prints `0 2 4 6`. The version that starts count at 1 does not match "Set count to 0" and prints only `2 4`.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain:
A do-while runs its body before it tests anything.
```
n = 10
body:  prints 10, then n++ makes n 11
test:  11 < 5 is false, so the loop ends
```
The output is `10`. If you answered that nothing prints, you treated it as a while loop, which would test `10 < 5` first and skip the body. In a do-while the test is not looked at until the first pass is done, so the body always runs at least once.

questions.prompt: The do-while loop is called a ____ loop because it tests its condition after the body.
questions.explain: The do-while is a posttest loop. "Post" means after: the condition is tested after each pass through the body. Because nothing is tested before the first pass, the body always runs at least once. The while loop is the opposite, a pretest loop, which tests first and can run zero times. Example: `do { cout << "hi"; } while (false);` still prints hi once.

questions.prompt: A do-while statement must end with a semicolon after the closing parenthesis of its condition.
questions.explain: True. A do-while ends with `} while (condition);` and the semicolon is required, because that line is the end of the whole statement. Without it the program does not compile. g++ reports an error such as "expected ';' before ...". The while loop is the opposite: a semicolon right after `while (condition)` compiles but creates an empty body, which usually means an infinite loop.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this loop?
choices: There is no semicolon after the while condition
The body should not use braces
The condition must come before the word do
x++ cannot be used in a do-while
questions.explain:
The do-while ends with `} while (x < 5)` and no semicolon. A do-while must end `} while (condition);`, because that line closes the whole statement. Without the semicolon the code does not compile.

The other complaints are wrong. Braces around the body are allowed, and needed when the body has more than one statement. In a do-while the condition belongs after the body, not before the word `do`. And `x++` is fine in any loop.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of times the body of a do-while loop executes?
choices: It depends on the condition
questions.explain:
At least 1 time. The body runs first and the condition is tested only afterwards, so the first pass happens no matter what the condition says.

"0" is the answer for a while loop, which tests first and can skip the body. "2" has no basis: if the first test is false, the loop stops after one pass. "It depends on the condition" is half true: the condition decides how many passes come after the first one, but it cannot stop the first one, so the minimum is still 1.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain:
Take the two loops one at a time. i starts at 5.
```
while (i < 5)    5 < 5 is false at the first test, body skipped
do-while body    prints B, i++ makes i 6
test i < 5       6 < 5 is false, loop ends
cout << i        prints 6
```
The output is `B6`, with no space between them. No A is printed because the while loop tests first. The B prints once because the do-while runs its body before testing.

questions.prompt: A program shows a menu and must display it at least once before testing whether the user chose Quit. Which loop fits best?
choices: while
a for loop that repeats exactly 5 times
do-while
a nested loop
questions.explain:
The do-while fits best. The menu must appear at least once before there is a choice to test, and a do-while runs its body (show the menu, read the choice) before it tests whether the choice was Quit.

A while loop tests first, so you would have to show the menu once before the loop as well, or set the choice to a fake value. A for loop that repeats exactly 5 times takes the decision away from the user: the menu should repeat until they choose Quit, however many times that is. A nested loop is a loop inside another loop, and it does not address showing the menu first.

questions.prompt: Which loop does exactly the same thing as the do-while below for ANY starting value of k?
choices: while (k < 6) { cout << k; k += 2; }
while (k < 6) { k += 2; cout << k; }
do { k += 2; cout << k; } while (k < 6);

cout << k; k += 2;
while (k < 6) { cout << k; k += 2; }
questions.explain:
A do-while is one copy of the body that always runs, followed by a while loop. The matching choice writes `cout << k; k += 2;` once and then the same while loop. It gives the same output for every starting k.

Check the others with test values. If k starts at 6, the do-while prints 6, but the plain `while (k < 6)` version prints nothing, because it tests first. If k starts at 0, the do-while prints 0, 2 and 4 (shown as `024`, since nothing separates them). Both versions that do `k += 2` before `cout` print 2, 4 and 6 (`246`), because they print the value after it has changed.

questions.prompt: A flowchart is described this way: Start, set n to 3, process box Display n, process box Subtract 1 from n, diamond 'n > 0?' with Yes going back to Display n and No going to End. Which C++ matches?
questions.explain:
In this flowchart the two process boxes come first and the diamond comes after them, with Yes looping back up. Diamond at the bottom means a do-while: `do { cout << n << " "; n--; } while (n > 0);`. It prints `3 2 1`.

The others: the while version that decrements before printing gives `2 1 0`. The version with a semicolon after `while (n > 0)` has an empty body and loops forever without printing. The do-while that tests `n < 0` prints 3, then `2 < 0` is false, so it stops after one pass.

questions.prompt: The second expression in a for loop header, which decides whether the body runs again, is called the ____ expression.
questions.explain: It is the test expression. A for header holds three parts separated by semicolons: initialization, test, update. In `for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)` the test is `i < 10`. It is checked before every pass, including the first. When it is true the body runs, and when it is false the loop ends, just like the condition of a while loop.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.code:
for (int i = 2; i <= 10; i += 4)
    cout << i << " ";
questions.explain:
List the values i takes. It starts at 2 and goes up by 4.
```
i = 2    2 <= 10 true    prints 2
i = 6    6 <= 10 true    prints 6
i = 10   10 <= 10 true   prints 10
i = 14   14 <= 10 false  loop ends
```
Output: `2 6 10`. 10 is printed because the test is `<=`, and 10 is equal to 10. With `i < 10` the loop would print only `2 6`.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body of this loop run?
questions.explain:
The body runs 4 times. List the values of i, adding 3 each time:
```
i = 0    0 < 10 true     runs is 1
i = 3    3 < 10 true     runs is 2
i = 6    6 < 10 true     runs is 3
i = 9    9 < 10 true     runs is 4
i = 12   12 < 10 false   loop ends
```
"3" forgets either the first pass at 0 or the pass at 9. "10" counts as if the step were 1. "5" counts the value 12 as well, but 12 fails the test, so its pass never happens.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain:
The loop counts down. The test `i > 0` is checked before each pass.
```
i = 3   3 > 0 true    prints 3
i = 2   true          prints 2
i = 1   true          prints 1
i = 0   0 > 0 false   loop ends
```
Then `cout << "Go"` runs once, after the loop. Output: `3 2 1 Go`. 0 is not printed, because the test fails before the body can run with i at 0.

questions.prompt: What happens with this code?
questions.code:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }
cout << i;
choices: It prints 3
It prints 2
It does not compile, because i is out of scope after the loop
It prints 0
questions.explain:
It does not compile. `int i = 0` is declared in the for header, so i exists only inside the loop: the header and the body. After the loop the name i is gone, and `cout << i;` fails with "'i' was not declared in this scope".

"It prints 3" would be right if i had been declared before the loop, as in `int i; for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }`. Then the loop would end with i at 3, the first value that fails the test. "2" and "0" are not the final value in any version.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain:
Here x is declared before the loop, so it still exists afterwards. The loop body is empty: the loop only moves x.
```
x = 0    0 < 20 true
x = 6    6 < 20 true
x = 12   12 < 20 true
x = 18   18 < 20 true
x = 24   24 < 20 false, loop ends
```
`cout << x` prints `24`. The tempting answer is 18, the last value that passed the test. But the update runs once more after the pass with 18, and the loop ends holding the first value that failed.

questions.prompt: All three expressions in a for loop header are optional, and `for (;;)` is a loop that runs until something like break stops it.
questions.explain: True. Each of the three parts of a for header may be left out, as long as both semicolons stay. Leaving out the initialization works when the variable was given its value before the loop. A missing update means the body must change things. A missing test counts as true, so `for (;;)` never ends by itself. Something inside the body has to stop it, such as a `break` statement or a `return`.

questions.prompt: Which while loop prints exactly the same thing as `for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) cout << i << " ";`?
questions.explain:
To turn a for loop into a while loop, move the initialization before the loop, keep the test as the while condition, and put the update at the END of the body. That gives `int i = 1;` then `while (i <= 5)` with `cout` first and `i++` last. It prints `1 2 3 4 5`.

The version with `i++` before the `cout` prints `2 3 4 5 6`, because each value is printed after it has changed. The version starting at 0 prints an extra 0. The do-while with `i < 5` stops after printing 4, because 5 < 5 is false.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.code:
for (int lo = 0, hi = 5; lo < hi; lo++, hi--)
    cout << lo << hi << " ";
questions.explain:
The commas let the header set up and update two variables. lo goes up and hi goes down on each pass.
```
lo = 0, hi = 5   0 < 5 true   prints 05
lo = 1, hi = 4   1 < 4 true   prints 14
lo = 2, hi = 3   2 < 3 true   prints 23
lo = 3, hi = 2   3 < 2 false  loop ends
```
`cout << lo << hi` prints the two numbers with nothing between them, then a space follows. Output: `05 14 23`.

questions.prompt: How many times does the statement `count++;` run? (The program prints count at the end.)
choices: It is an infinite loop
questions.explain:
Look at the end of the header: `for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++);`. That semicolon is an empty statement, and it is the whole body of the loop. The loop runs 3 times doing nothing, then ends. `count++;` comes after it, so it runs exactly once, and the program prints 1. The indentation only makes it look as if it is inside.

"3" would be right without the stray semicolon. "0" assumes `count++` is inside a loop that never runs. It is not an infinite loop, because the update `i++` still runs on each pass and i reaches 3.

questions.prompt: Which header displays 10 9 8 ... 3 2 1 when the body is `cout << i << " ";`?
choices: for (int i = 10; i > 1; i--)
for (int i = 10; i >= 1; i--)
for (int i = 10; i <= 1; i--)
for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i--)
questions.explain:
To print 10 down to 1, start at 10, subtract 1 each pass, and use a test that is still true when i is 1: `for (int i = 10; i >= 1; i--)`.

With `i > 1` the test fails when i reaches 1, so it prints 10 down to 2 and misses 1. With `i <= 1` the first test is `10 <= 1`, which is false, so nothing prints. Starting at 1 with `i--` moves i down to 0, -1, -2 and so on, away from 10. The test `i <= 10` stays true and the loop never ends.

questions.prompt:
Complete the header so it visits 0, 5, 10, ... 100:
`for (int n = 0; n <= 100; ____)`
questions.explain:
